readerTitle: The design team that lost its monopoly
caseNote: 가상 사례 (사내 디자인팀, 버블티 가게, 냉장 창고) + 실제 관찰 (시멘트 산업의 진입 장벽) + 개념 출처 (Porter의 다섯 가지 힘)
insight: 이익을 지켜주는 것은 지금의 경쟁자가 약하다는 사실이 아니라, 새로운 누군가가 시작하기 얼마나 어려운가이다. 진입이 쉬우면 아무도 들어오지 않아도 가격과 서비스가 이미 제한된다.
misconception: 지금 경쟁자가 없으면 가격을 마음대로 올려도 안전하다. 진입 장벽이 있으면 이익은 영원히 지켜진다.

sources.text: Porter, M. (1979). How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy. Harvard Business Review.
Porter, M. (2008). The Five Competitive Forces That Shape Strategy. Harvard Business Review.
사내 디자인팀, 버블티 가게, 냉장 창고 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 진입 장벽 분류(규모의 경제, 초기 자본, 유통·공급 접근, 전환 비용, 브랜드·노하우, 규제)가 Porter(1979, 2008)의 분류와 맞는지 게시 전에 확인하세요. 카드에는 쉬운 표현으로 묶어 적었습니다.
시멘트 산업 설명(큰 초기 투자, 인허가, 원료 채석장 근접 필요, 무거워서 장거리 운송 비용이 높아 시장이 지역 단위)은 일반적인 산업 관찰로 적었습니다. 특정 국가나 기업 수치는 넣지 않았습니다. 표현이 과하지 않은지 확인하세요.
사내 디자인팀의 3주 대기, 냉장 창고 200km 등 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: The design team that lost its monopoly
body: For years, every slide, flyer and banner at the company went through one central design team. The queue was three weeks long, and nobody had another option.
Then marketing hired its own designer. Sales started making flyers with an online template tool. Nobody announced a rival team. One simply appeared.

image.label: Office desks with a long queue of requests at one team and a new desk appearing nearby
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일 사무실. 한 팀 책상 앞에 요청서 더미가 길게 쌓여 있고, 옆 부서에 새 책상과 노트북이 막 놓이는 장면. 화면 속 디자인 툴은 가상의 인터페이스로, 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Marketing wants its own designer.
body: You lead the central design team. Requests wait three weeks. The head of marketing has asked finance for budget to hire a designer of their own.

options.text: Ask leadership for a rule that all design work must go through your team
options.feedback: A rule can block the new hire for now. But it fixes nothing about the wait, and rules can be reversed as soon as enough people complain.

options.text: Cut the wait: templates and a fast lane for simple jobs, your team for complex brand work
options.feedback: You give up the easy jobs, but you remove the main reason to go elsewhere and focus on work that is hard to copy.

options.text: Let them hire. Less work for your team
options.feedback: It eases the queue today. But budget and influence follow the work, and other departments will likely do the same.

cards.title: The wall was lower than it looked.
body: The design team assumed it was safe. Good design needed skilled people and expensive software.

But template tools made simple jobs easy for anyone, and one hire could cover a department's basics. Within a year, the central team handled a fraction of the company's design work, and its budget shrank with it.
Its protection had never been its quality. It was how hard it used to be to start.

cards.title: The threat of new entrants
body: **New entrants** are competitors who could start serving your customers. The size of the threat depends on **barriers to entry**: whatever makes starting hard, slow or costly.
The twist: the threat works before anyone arrives. When starting is easy, high prices or slow service act as an invitation. Your profits are capped by what it would take for someone new to show up.

image.label: A wall around a field of coins, with a newcomer measuring its height
image.brief: 인포그래픽 스타일. 동전이 쌓인 들판을 낮은 담이 둘러싸고, 바깥에서 한 사람이 줄자로 담 높이를 재는 장면. 담에 "Barriers to entry" 라벨. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Where barriers come from
body: Most barriers fall into a few groups:
list: **Scale:** big players have lower costs per unit that a newcomer can't match at first
**Money up front:** factories, fleets, stores or equipment
**Access:** suppliers, shelf space, routes or locations already taken
**Switching costs:** customers lose time or money by changing
**Know-how and trust:** skills and reputation take years to build
cards.callout: Ask which of these a newcomer could buy, rent or skip.
cards.softwareNote: Building software is cheaper than ever, so barriers rarely come from the product itself. They come from switching costs, integrations, data and networks of users that a new product can't copy on day one.

cards.title: A bubble tea shop and a cement plant
body: Picture a block where one bubble tea shop has a line out the door. A lease, a few machines and a menu are enough to start, so within a year three more open nearby. Prices drift down and the line splits four ways.

Now picture a cement plant. It needs a huge investment, permits and a nearby quarry, and cement is too heavy to ship far cheaply. Few newcomers try, so local producers usually face little new competition.

image.label: Four tea shops on one block beside a single cement plant
image.brief: 좌우 분할 일러스트. 왼쪽은 한 블록에 비슷한 버블티 가게 네 곳이 나란히 있는 거리, 오른쪽은 채석장 옆에 홀로 선 시멘트 공장. 가게 간판은 가상의 이름이나 무늬만, 실제 브랜드 없음.

cards.title: Barriers move.
body: Barriers wear down. New tools, cheaper equipment or a change in rules can turn a high wall into a step, as the design team found.
The most dangerous entrants often come from next door: a customer who decides to do the work itself, or a large company from a nearby industry that already has the money and the customers.
And a barrier is not a license to overcharge. The bigger your profits, the more a newcomer can afford to spend getting over the wall.

cards.title: Now it's a cold-storage warehouse.
body: You run the only refrigerated warehouse within 200 km. Local food producers pay you well, and your margins are high. Your largest customer mentions it is pricing out a warehouse of its own.

options.text: Raise rates. They have nowhere else to go
options.feedback: You earn more this year, but you hand the customer a stronger case for building. Once built, that warehouse may take your other customers too.

options.text: Keep rates fair, offer a multi-year deal and add services like inventory tracking
options.feedback: You give up some short-term margin, but you shrink the payoff from building and raise the cost of leaving. That protects the profit you keep.

options.text: Relax. Nobody spends millions on a warehouse just to save on fees
options.feedback: Upfront cost is a real barrier. But a big customer with big bills can justify the build, and your high margins are exactly what make it pay.

cards.title: Your profits are limited by who could show up.
body: Look past today's rivals. Ask how hard it would be for someone new, including your own customers, to start doing what you do.
**Try it today:** list three things a newcomer would need to compete with you. Mark the ones they could buy or rent within six months.
